newsitem.title: GERMANY: German conservatives take aim at foreign workers.
newsitem.headline: German conservatives take aim at foreign workers.

text.p: Germany's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), casting aside fears about inflaming racist sentiments, called on Wednesday for stricter limits on foreign workers as part of their new strategy to cut unemployment.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, chairman of the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said it was "grotesque" that millions of Germans were unemployed while so many foreigners were working here.
CSU parliamentary leader Michael Glos said the system was at fault if more than four million Germans were jobless while more than one million foreigners received work permits each year.

"We have the problem of high unemployment among Germans but at the same time we employ many foreigners," Waigel said in an interview with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper. "It should be legitimate to look at ways to make sure Germans get the jobs."
The CSU, the most right-wing of Germany's mainstream parties and a junior partner in Kohl's ruling coalition, has long been noted for its arch-conservative views.

But the Bavarians and other major parties have long refrained from directly linking the high 10 percent unemployment level to the eight million foreign residents, in part because they want to avoid being accused of fomenting racial unrest.
They have been especially careful since xenophobic violence erupted in Germany in the early 1990s.

"It is schizophrenic that we give so many jobs to foreigners each year only because Germans don't want to do this work," Waigel said. "German employers keep telling us they need, for example, seasonal workers from Poland. I call that grotesque."

Glos, who has recently been preparing the ground for the party's efforts to propose legislation to tighten restrictions on foreigners, told ARD television the party's aim was to stop the immigration of foreigners from outside the European Union.
"It is wrong that in Germany certain jobs are only filled by non-EU foreigners," he said. "That makes it appear as if these tasks can only be done by slaves from somewhere else."
Waigel and Glos were speaking just before the CSU starts an annual three-day party conference in a castle in the Bavarian village of Wildbad Kreuth.

Glos said the party leaders would discuss the proposed restrictions on foreigners, along with other legislative initiatives, during the conference, but he emphasised that no decisions on limits had yet been reached.
Glos said the proposals were designed to force unemployed Germans to accept jobs they have until now been turning down.
The comments came as Bild daily reported there are 109,000 unemployed restaurant workers in Germany at the same time as there are 190,000 unfilled vacancies.
The paper also found jobs involving heavy labour such as cleaning, or working in the iron, fishing or textile industries were filled with a disproprionately high number of foreigners.
